characters: Odarkor: a boy of four with round cheeks, a red T-shirt and shorts, with a bobbing head of curls.
Adjeley: his sister, aged ten, in a school uniform, holding his hand.
The road: a busy road with a zebra crossing, a bus, a taxi and a motorbike, drawn with a pavement on each side.

narrationPlan.voice: A cheerful big sister’s voice, with an excited little boy
narrationPlan.pace: Rhythmic and clear, with a steady beat on “Stop, Look, Listen” (about 85 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: A bouncy beat with hand claps and a bell on every “Stop” (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Odarkor and Adjeley are invented. The story teaches a simple crossing routine: stop at the edge, look both ways, listen, wait until the road is clear, walk (do not run) and hold a grown-up’s hand.

The story does not say which way to look first, so that it is correct wherever children live. Teachers should practise the routine at a real, safe crossing with an adult and point out zebra crossings, pavements and lights where they exist.
The story does not show any child crossing alone.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Have a road safety officer check that the routine (stop, look both ways, listen, wait, walk, hold a hand) is correct for Ghana and for this age group.
Check that a child of ten is shown as a helper and not as a replacement for an adult for young children.

teacherGuide.overview: A rhythm story that teaches a simple road-crossing routine. Children say and act out “Stop, look, listen”.
learningGoals: Say the three steps of crossing safely.
Say why we hold a grown-up’s hand.
beforeReading: Ask: how do you get to school? Do you cross a road?
whileReading: Stamp softly on “Stop”, turn heads on “Look” and cup ears on “Listen”.
afterReading: Practise with a floor road, with a “zebra crossing” made of tape, and a toy bus.
Walk to a real crossing with adults and practise the routine.
discussion: What should you do when you see a bus coming?
reflection: Who holds your hand when you cross a road?

support: Use picture cards for stop, look and listen.
stretch: Draw a road with a safe crossing and label what the children do.

culturalNotes: Odarkor and Adjeley are invented. The story teaches a simple crossing routine: stop at the edge, look both ways, listen, wait until the road is clear, walk (do not run) and hold a grown-up’s hand.

The story does not say which way to look first, so that it is correct wherever children live. Teachers should practise the routine at a real, safe crossing with an adult and point out zebra crossings, pavements and lights where they exist.
The story does not show any child crossing alone.
localiseThis: Use the crossing, bus or taxi children really see. Never let children practise on a real road without adults.

factCheck.claim: Children should stop at the edge of the road, look both ways, listen, wait until it is clear, walk across and hold an adult’s hand.
factCheck.explanation: Standard road-safety guidance for young children.
